query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying an Al2O3-based protective coating to a metal substrate can improve oxidation resistance by forming a stable oxide barrier that reduces oxygen diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: Metal alloy substrate (e.g., Ni-based superalloy) without any surface coating
generation.intervention: Deposition of an Al2O3 coating via thermal spray or chemical vapor deposition
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidative environment (e.g., temperatures up to 1100 °C in air)
generation.structural_mediator: Dense adherent Al2O3 film on the alloy surface
generation.mechanism: A stable Al2O3 layer inhibits direct contact between oxygen and the substrate, thereby decreasing oxidation and slowing alloy degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significantly reduced oxidation rate and enhanced component lifetime relative to uncoated alloys
generation.baseline: Uncoated metal alloys at elevated temperatures exhibit faster oxide growth, loss of structural integrity, and shorter service life
generation.boundary: Potential coating failure in highly corrosive environments (e.g., sulfur- or chlorine-containing atmospheres) or under extreme thermal cycling
generation.uncertainty: Performance data are limited for long-term cyclic oxidation in complex service conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a comparative oxidation test in which coated and uncoated metal alloy samples are heated to 1100 °C in air for several hundred hours and periodically weighed to measure mass changes.
measurements: Mass gain due to oxide growth
Surface morphology and oxide spallation via scanning electron microscopy
Composition of oxide scale using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is contradicted if the coated samples show equivalent or greater mass gain and oxide spallation relative to uncoated controls under the same conditions.
